prerequisites: It is recommended to have completed Physics I and Physics II, as they may be useful for the development of some concepts used in this course.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of the basic concepts related to Fluid Mechanics and the main properties and phenomena that are representative of fluids.

Handling of the basic laws of Fluid Statics and their application to the study of pressure distribution over a surface: pressure diagram, moment of inertia of a surface, center of gravity and center of pressure; application to the equilibrium of gates and associated calculations.
Knowledge of the basic conservation laws and their application to mass, energy, linear momentum, and angular momentum balances.

Ability to analyze water distribution systems by applying mass and energy balances, with corresponding calculations related to the determination of fluid head and power, as well as head losses associated with pipes and accessories.
Knowledge of the concept of hydrodynamic boundary layer and ability to perform basic calculations related to the resistance to relative motion between a surface and a fluid.
Handling of concepts related to dimensional analysis and model similarity and ability to perform associated basic calculations.
Ability to analyze water distribution systems that include pumps, pipe associations, and/or in-route service.
Ability to simulate installations using EPANET software.
Ability to structure the resolution of a problem systematically.
Ability to combine individual autonomy with collaborative group work.
Ability for adequate organization and planning of work.
Ability for autonomous learning, being able to learn what is necessary to solve a problem.
Ability to prepare a written report with formal rigor.
Ability to formulate and apply simplifying hypotheses to problem solving.
Ability for critical analysis of results, being able to detect calculation errors or modify working hypotheses.
Knowledge of basic and technological matters, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing versatility to adapt to new situations.

Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning, and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Industrial Mechanical Engineering.
Ability to work in a multilingual and multidisciplinary environment.
Ability to analyze and synthesize.
Ability to organize and plan time.
Ability for written expression.
Ability to solve problems.
Ability for critical reasoning/logical analysis.

syllabus_topics: Section I. Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics
Chapter 1. General concepts and fluid properties
Definitions and classifications typical of Fluid Mechanics. Newton's law, viscosity, and shear stress. Flow profiles in laminar and turbulent regimes. Cavitation.
Chapter 2. Fluid Statics

Definition of pressure and its properties. Fundamental equation of statics. Pressure diagrams: decomposition into elementary sections. Calculation of forces on surfaces (center of gravity). Calculation of moments (center of pressure). Moment of inertia of a surface.
Chapter 3. General Equations of Fluid Mechanics

Flow energy (head, power): elevation, pressure, and kinetic terms. Head losses. Mass balance: continuity equation. Energy balance: Bernoulli's equation and its generalization. Momentum balance: calculation of forces in short ducts (elbows, bifurcations, nozzles).
Chapter 4. Dimensional Analysis and Similarity
Fundamentals of dimensional analysis. Characteristic dimensionals of Fluid Mechanics and their scope of application. Similarity conditions.
Chapter 5. Flow Resistance: Boundary Layer
Concept of boundary layer. Boundary layer of a flat plate. Surface resistance. Boundary layer separation. Form resistance and total resistance.
Section II. Applications of Fluid Mechanics to Engineering
Chapter 6. Resistance in Conduits

General equation for head losses in conduits. Head losses in pipes: Darcy-Weissbach equation. Friction coefficient in pipes: Colebrook equation and Moody diagram. Secondary head losses: changes in section, tank inlet and outlet, valves and other accessories. Head losses in channels.
Chapter 7. Fundamentals of Hydraulic Circuits and Distribution Systems
Series and parallel connection of pipes. Pipes with in-route service (supply from one or two ends). Energy analysis of installations with pumps.
Problem P1. Analysis and Sizing of a Counterweight System for a Sluice Gate / Analysis of an Experimental System for Measuring the Center of Pressure
Problem P2. Analysis and Sizing of a Water Supply System for an Irrigation and Spraying System
Problem P3. Water Supply to a Population via In-Route Service
EPANET Seminar: initiation to the use of this free software tool developed by the US Environmental Protection Agency.
Laboratory Practice 1. Study of a liquid in rotation
Laboratory Practice 2. Measurement of forces on surfaces
Laboratory Practice 3. Measurements of head losses
Laboratory Practice 4. Use of diagrams for determining head losses
Laboratory Practice 5. EPANET simulation of basic water distribution systems
Laboratory Practice 6. Analysis of a Venturi
teaching_methods: Exercises from recommended bibliography and virtual classroom
Error analysis and concept review classes
Use of specific software (EPANET) or general software (spreadsheet)
Academic-formative tutorials (seminars for lab practices, EPANET introduction)
Use of virtual classroom for information and communication
Use of bibliography and reading documents in English
Handling EPANET software in its original English version
assessment_rules: The course grade is determined by continuous assessment (EC) in the first attempt, or by single assessment (EU) for subsequent attempts or by student choice. To pass the course, a minimum grade of 5.0 or higher is required in both the 'Problem Solving' block (65%) and the 'Laboratory Practices' block (35%). The Final Exam (50% of the course grade) consists of two parts: Part I (40% of the exam) requires a minimum score of 4.0 for Part II (60% of the exam) to be graded, and Part II also requires a minimum score of 4.0 to be averaged with Part I (otherwise, the maximum exam score is 4.0). Laboratory practices require an 'APTO' (pass), which entails mandatory attendance at all preparation activities and satisfactory completion of all 6 practices (at least 5.0). If the final exam is failed, the course grade will be 'Fail' regardless of other grades, and 'Not Presented' if the exam is not taken.
